title_en: The Passion of Marian and James
author: Anonymous
addressee: Christian brethren: the fraternity and people of God
occasion: At Marianus and James's own request (instinctu spiritus caelestis inierunt... in notitiam fraternitatis per nos uenire iusserunt) the narrator, their intimate companion, records their contest not to boast of their crown on earth but so the people may be armed by their example for faith.
argument: Humble martyrs racing for the heavenly kingdom ask their friend to publish their struggle so others learn steadfastness (instinctu spiritus caelestis inierunt... in notitiam fraternitatis per nos uenire iusserunt). Arrested near Cirta during a fierce persecution, James, a deacon who had survived the attacks (infestationes) of the Decian persecution once already (infestationes iam semel Decianae persecutionis euicerat) and volunteers confession as deacon, and Marianus, who confessed himself only a lector (lectorem tantum), which made him subject to torments, confess Christ, suffer hanging torture, and endure prison with prayer. In prison they and fellow-prisoner Aemilianus receive visions confirming approaching execution, unequal heavenly rewards differentiated like stars' varying brightness, yet one light for all (Numquid stella omnis pari luminis honore praefulget? Et tamen lumen omnibus unum est), and welcome by Cyprian specifically (Cyprianus apparuit et porrexit manum et leuauit me in altiorem catastae locum); Agapius appears separately in James's dream. After delay while many lay Christians are executed, the clerics are condemned and beheaded together by a river outside the city, with signs of light, white horsemen, and Marianus prophesying coming judgments, to the joy of Marianus's mother.

outline.move: The narrator accepts the martyrs' modest commission to publish their struggle as an example for the brethren.
Traveling together in Numidia to Muguas near Cirta, they find persecution raging under a bloody governor seeking Christians including exiled confessors.

Bishops Agapius and Secundinus, led from exile toward death, lodge with the narrator and strengthen all by teaching and example; they are described as already crowned martyrs in mind (mente iam martyras) though not yet by blood.
Two days later soldiers come seeking Marianus and James at the villa; they voluntarily follow to Cirta with others, openly confess Christianity, and are imprisoned after interrogation.

Examined with military and civic cruelty, James volunteers confession as deacon (not merely Christian), while Marianus's confession as lector makes him subject to torments; Marianus survives hanging by thumbs with weights and returns rejoicing to prison.
Marianus recounts his night vision of a high white tribunal, stepped scaffold, a judge ordering execution, and Cyprian raising him to sit beside him and giving him spring water in a paradise garden.
James recalls his midday cart-journey vision of a huge shining youth above the clouds giving each of them a purple belt and calling them to follow quickly.

Fellow prisoner Aemilianus recounts his midday dream-dialogue with his pagan carnal brother (homo gentilis, hoc est frater meus carnalis) about light in darkness, coming capital punishment (poena capitalis), unequal rewards like stars, two greater ones unnamed, and the camel through the needle's eye.

Brought out publicly with honorable records of confession (elogio fortissimae confessionis honoratos), they gain another confessor by example, are sent on to the governor, and received into prison at Lambaesis (Lambesitanus carcer).

While many lay Christians are executed first through a policy separating laity from clergy (artifex saeuitia diuiserat), the imprisoned clerics grieve at their slow and late victory (tam lenta et tam sera uictoria).

James dreams that Agapius feasts joyfully and a rose-crowned twin child (alterum ex geminis, one of twins) with a green palm promises they will dine together tomorrow, and next day they are sentenced and led to a river valley between hills to be baptized in their own blood and washed in the river.

In a methodical mass beheading with eyes veiled by custom (de more) at the sword-blow, the martyrs see light and white horses with white-clad youths (some seeing, some recognizing by sound), and Marianus prophesies plague, captivity, famine, earthquake and stinging flies (cynomiae uenena cruciantia) as vengeance.
Marianus's mother, called Mary, embraces his body and neck-wounds with Maccabean joy, closed by doxology to God.

cast.name: Marian
cast.who: Lector and central martyr, companion of the narrator and James

cast.name: James
cast.who: Deacon, fellow martyr and intimate of Marianus, who had survived the attacks (infestationes) of the Decian persecution once already

cast.name: Agapius
cast.who: Bishop led from exile to martyrdom who had prayed for Tertulla and Antonia

cast.name: Secundinus
cast.who: Bishop and fellow exile martyred with Agapius

cast.name: Cyprian
cast.who: Bishop martyred at Carthage 258 CE, who appears in Marianus's vision to raise and welcome him (date of Cyprian's martyrdom not stated in text)

cast.name: Aemilianus
cast.who: Though held to be of equestrian order in pagan estimation (quamuis equestris ordinis gentiliter haberetur), one of the brothers in prison, who in continence of the flesh had come to nearly his fiftieth year as a boy (puer)

cast.name: Tertulla
cast.who: Young girl beloved by Agapius, for whom he prayed she become a martyr

cast.name: Antonia
cast.who: Young girl beloved by Agapius, for whom he prayed she become a martyr

cast.name: Mary, mother of Marian
cast.who: Marianus's mother who rejoices over his body after execution

cast.name: The governor, unnamed
cast.who: Persecuting provincial governor at Cirta and Lambaesis

cast.name: Twin boy, unnamed, with his mother
cast.who: One of twins (alterum ex geminis) martyred three days earlier with his mother who appears promising a heavenly banquet tomorrow

voices.how_marked: direct address quoted as Veni, sede mecum

voices.how_marked: waking report introduced with inquit and Vidi, inquit

key_terms.sense: those who die, or are about to die, for confessing Christ; already called so before death
candidates: witnesses who die for their faith

key_terms.sense: open public avowal I am a Christian, with office when pressed
heavenly reward and victory for completed suffering, not earthly boasting
God's gracious favor permitting suffering, visions and martyrdom
Roman provincial governor directing persecution and sentence
high stepped platform where the condemned are shown then sent to death
official record of charge and steadfast confession sent with prisoners to the governor
lower clerical office Marianus holds, publicly avowed under torture
clerical office James insists on avowing beyond merely Christian
bishops Agapius and Secundinus as illustrious priests and models
heavenly love-feast to which martyrs are invited after death
binding Christian pledge and shared holy life, also holy rites fulfilled in blood and water

scripture: No psalms are quoted and no LXX or Vulgate book-titles occur; the only formal scriptural sentence is the camel through the needle's eye, in Old Latin wording. Cite it in modern form as Matthew 19:24 (parallels Mark 10:25; Luke 18:25). The closing Maccabean joy is an allusion to 2 Maccabees 7, not a citation; do not supply chapter-verse for allusions.
uncertain: Narrator's personal name is not given in the text, only intimacy and shared travel and lodging
Exact year and governor's name are not stated in the text; 259 under Valerian rests on external tradition
Location Muguas and the river execution site are not further identified in the text
Whether vision dialogues reproduce exact words or summary is not stated
Psalm numbering and Latin Bible version cannot be established because no psalm is cited

_unresolved_facts.claim: Tertulla... Young girl beloved by Agapius, for whom he prayed she become a martyr
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: cum pro puellis duabus, Tertulla et Antonia, quas sibi carissimas ad uicem pignerum diligebat, repetitis frequenter precibus oraret ut secum et illae dei dignatione martyres fierent
_unresolved_facts.fix: Tertulla... One of two girls (puellae) whom Agapius loved as dear to him in place of pledges (ad uicem pignerum), for whom he prayed that by God's grace they might become martyrs with him

_unresolved_facts.claim: Antonia... Young girl beloved by Agapius, for whom he prayed she become a martyr
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: cum pro puellis duabus, Tertulla et Antonia, quas sibi carissimas ad uicem pignerum diligebat, repetitis frequenter precibus oraret ut secum et illae dei dignatione martyres fierent
_unresolved_facts.fix: Antonia... One of two girls (puellae) whom Agapius loved as dear to him in place of pledges (ad uicem pignerum), for whom he prayed that by God's grace they might become martyrs with him

_unresolved_facts.claim: Twin boy, unnamed, with his mother... One of twins (alterum ex geminis) martyred three days earlier with his mother who appears promising a heavenly banquet tomorrow
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: puer, quem constabat esse alterum ex geminis ante triduum cum matre conpassis, corona rosea collo circumdatus
_unresolved_facts.fix: Twin boy, unnamed... One of twins (alterum ex geminis) who had suffered martyrdom (conpassis) three days before with his mother, appearing with rose crown and green palm promising they will dine together tomorrow

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ["3"]... Bishops Agapius and Secundinus, led from exile toward death, lodge with the narrator and strengthen all by teaching and example; they are described as already crowned martyrs in mind (mente iam martyras) though not yet by blood
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: in illos quoque manum diabolus insatiabilem porrigebat, quos iamdudum in exilia submotos, etsi nondum sanguine, mente iam martyras, ferox praesidis amentia coronarat
_unresolved_facts.fix: The description of those already crowned martyrs in mind (mente iam martyras) refers to unnamed exiled confessors in section 2, not specifically to Agapius and Secundinus in section 3; section 3 describes Agapius and Secundinus as bishops led from exile, lodging with the narrator, and strengthening others

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ["10"]... While many lay Christians are executed first through a policy separating laity from clergy (artifex saeuitia diuiserat), the imprisoned clerics grieve at their slow and late victory (tam lenta et tam sera uictoria)
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: laicorum tam multis occupata uulneribus... Ergo carissimi nostri et fidelissimi milites Christi ceterique de clero contristari aliquantulum coeperant, quod, laicis certaminis sui laude perfunctis, seruaretur sibi tam lenta et tam sera uictoria
_unresolved_facts.fix: The clerics grieve that their victory is kept so slow and late (tam lenta et tam sera uictoria) while lay people complete their contest's glory first; the policy separated laity from clergy in temptation and terror, not necessarily in execution order alone

_unresolved_facts.claim: James reporting his own dream of Agapius's banquet... night-vision report with inquit Iacobus and uidebam; James and Marianus are both raptured to the banquet in the dream
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Nam ista nocte, fratres, Agapium nostrum uidebam inter omnes alios laetiorem... Quo cum ego et Marianus quasi ad agapem spiritu dilectionis et caritatis raperemur
_unresolved_facts.fix: James reporting his own dream of Agapius's banquet... night-vision report with inquit Iacobus and uidebam; James and Marianus are both raptured (raperemur) to the banquet in the dream as if to an agape feast (quasi ad agapem)
